subtopic: DEBT SERVICING AND REDUCTION ACCOUNT ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, September 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-21, an Act relating to the accounting of certain payments for the servicing and reduction of the debt of Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: DEBT SERVICING AND REDUCTION ACCOUNT ACT
speechtext: The hon. member for Ontario has 16 minutes left. The hon. member for Ontario.

subtopic: DEBT SERVICING AND REDUCTION ACCOUNT ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to continue debate on this bill which we started on Wednesday. At that time I made some comments relative to some past performances and will cariy on from where I left off.
What we are talking about is taking all of the revenues of the goods and services tax, revenues from the sale of various Crown corporations and other gifts to Canada and putting them aside specifically targeted and earmarked to be put against the debt of Canada. It is with that in mind that I would like to carry on my comments.
We all have to appreciate and understand that we are not talking about one particular bill, although that is certainly the subject that is in front of us. We are talking about the over-all policies of the Government of Canada.
Without some of the other pieces of proposed legislation, this bill in itself would be ineffective. We have to control government spending. We have to keep the revenues of the government reasonably stable, and therefore, this bill will have some effect.
Another proposed piece of legislation that I am involved in is receiving some representations. It represents the dilemma that all Canadians face, certainly. I was involved in the hearings concerning the establishment of the goods and services tax, as well as back in my own constituency.
One of the fears of Canadians is that if this ends up being a "cash cow", the Government of Canada would simply create all kinds of new programs to spend all this new-found wealth, if we can describe it that way.
In my constituency, Canadians said: "We understand we have to pay the debt. We understand we have to address the deficit, and if you can assure us that the revenues you get from the GST will not be spent on new programs, that it will be used to address the debt, then, we might not like the goods and services tax, but we will be able to accept it much more readily because we all know that we have to sometime pay the bill." This bill does that.
To give you the alternative, in the finance committee hearings this week dealing with the control on government spending, we have had some excellent representations. I think it reflects the concern in the country because we had appear before us, a group called the Canadian Taxpayers' Federation.
I would just like to quote one paragraph from its representation: "We support the principle of the Spending Control Act because it represents the beginning of a solution to the prisoners' dilemma. While all of us collectively might agree that the federal government should reduce its deficit, each of us individually has been unwilling to suffer cuts to those programs from which we, as individuals, have benefitted".

I think that is very well said. Certainly in the last few days in the Windsor area, we have had another manifestation of the problem. We have had the truckers closing some transportation routes, demanding that the government cut taxes. They were demanding that this spring in my riding, the heart of where the trucking industry started the blockade in Ontario. They were demanding that the government cut taxes. That is one side of the coin: cut taxes. This groups says they collectively are not willing to absorb their share of that cut.
This week we have had in the finance committee an alternative presented to that of cutting taxes. That view was presented by the taxpayers' coalition about Canadians not willing to share their concern. In fact we have had people lined up trying to get their share of this "cash cow", if I can describe the GST as some others have.
To give you the best examples of the alternatives, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture this week appeared before the committee and said: "CFA is concerned that these programs will be considered under the new policy initiatives enrichment provision section which are not exempted from the proposed legislation and will therefore bring some cuts in other agricultural programs or elsewhere." It went on to talk about how it needed more money.
There was another group that appeared before us as well and that was the Canadian Association of University Teachers. I would like to quote a sentence from their presentation: "We also feel that the government is dangerously limiting its own room for manoeuvring in the years to come and we fear that once again higher education will be forced to pay the cost". Their presentation talked about how they needed more money.
Yesterday the National Action Committee on the Status of Women appeared before us. They came to comment about their perceptions with regard to child care. They had a tremendous program of additional demands for money from the federal government. You can see that just this week throughout this country the debate rages; one side saying do not spend it, cut taxes, and another side saying they want more money.
That is the dilemma we face and that is why I think we have made the right decision in dealing with the GST;
that the funds generated from the GST have to go into that special account and just cannot be spent anywhere.
It is not just the GST revenues. I would like to relate some other revenues that might be going into this debt servicing reduction account.
In the past the Government of Canada has sold off some corporations that we, collectively, paid for with Canadian taxes: Nordion Corporation, Air Canada, de Havilland, Canadair, just to name a few. The Canadian taxpayer, having paid for these corporations for all these years, when we sold them, where was the benefit to the taxpayer? Did we get a dividend? Did we get a reduction on our debt? We got nothing. The money was put somewhere in general revenues, and it disappeared. Nobody can identify specifically the dividend from our investment in that.
Let us look a little further because we are now embarked on the sale of a Crown corporation, Petro-Canada. Taxpayers have put a tremendous amount of money in that. I would think that when it is ultimately sold that Canadians would want to know that the money from the sale of the corporation has gone to reduce the debt that in fact was incurred when we purchased the corporation in the first place.
Could you imagine some other corporations that we might sell? Can you imagine selling CN Rail? Think of the billions of dollars that would generate if we ever got around to talking about selling it. The CBC-I am not sure anybody would want to buy that-but think of the potential revenue of selling CBC. VIA Rail is another Crown corporation we could get rid of that Canadians might be willing to buy privately. We could put all of that money, however much there might be, into reducing the debt that we incurred in owning those things in the first place.
How about the Royal Canadian Mint? Can you imagine if we sold that how much we could get for it? People might be interested in selling all of those things if they knew that when we sold them the revenue would be used to reduce the debt that was incurred.

Well, now we have heard from the Liberal Party opposite. They want to sell the House of Commons. That is the level of debate they put into this thing. They should know that the House of Commons is
September 20, 1991

not for sale. They have often tried to sell it, tried to get people to buy it with money but it is not for sale. Anyway, that is the process.
There is another program. In fact this week the Fraser Institute appeared before the finance committee and it talked about a program where they would establish a prize of $40,000 for the individual who could come up with the best savings each year in the operations of the Government of Canada without a commensurate reduction in the level of service. For any Canadian, whether it be a constituent from my riding or any other riding, or even a member of Parliament, who can come up with a particular program that will reduce costs without reducing level of service, there is a $40,000 prize. The member for Ottawa Centre, I believe, came up with a suggestion, as he put it, of a gift to the Government of Canada to reduce the debt that exists. Rather than have it spent someplace else, it would be donated. He retracted on that because he said: "Well, first we have to reduce the debt of the Liberal Party", so he would donate it there.
The idea is that there are people willing to make contributions to the Government of Canada to reduce the debts of this country. Rather than have it simply spent on some new program, have it spent somewhere in this country on some spending that may not be commensurate with the idea of the person who gave the money in the first place. We now have put in place a mechanism so that money just is not spent that comes out of it.
Now, you have also heard, Madam Speaker, all of these Canadians talk about the GST as a great generator of revenue. Well, that might be true but I guess we should look at the first four months of this fiscal year. I saw a report in The Globe and Mail this morning which suggested that net revenue on the GST to the end of July, which is the most recent available, amounts to about $4.6 billion. Our budget for the year is just over $16 billion. If this great generator of extra revenue is going to generate the billions that people are lining up to spend, they had better look at that July number again. It says that we are basically on target, that we are generating the revenue we said we would generate in the first year, and I think that is heartening to know.
More important, even though the facts do not yet point that way, if those who suggest this is a great generator of revenue are right, is it not great to know that this debt reduction fund account will be in place and it will prevent the Government of Canada from simply

creating a new program, from simply spending it someplace else? Very clearly, this money will be earmarked exactly where the constituents in my riding have said it should be. If we have to pay this tax, and if there is extra revenue, we want to know that the Government of Canada is not just going to frivolously spend it. That is what we will accomplish when we finally pass this bill.
The debt burden has been built up over years. Some 20 years has seen a tremendous amount of growth in that debt. There was some debt prior to the seventies, but basically it has been a growth of debt over the last 20 years. It is a result of Liberal spending and Conservative spending. It is a result of 15 or 16 years of deficits and compound interest on debt that existed over the years. So, that is there. How it got there I am sure all Canadians are aware.
But it has to stop. You cannot do it instantly, you cannot just wipe out that debt, you cannot just wipe out the deficit, because there are many Canadians who rely on the very important programs for their particular needs. So it will take many years of fiscal responsibility based on tough committed action to reduce the debt to a more manageable proportion.
I think the debt servicing and reduction account is a threshold step to make certain that we continue and accelerate and progress toward this vital goal that all Canadians have.
It was some 60 years ago that Prime Minister Mackenzie King told this House that "the promises of yesterday are the taxes of today". This legislation takes a different course. It is a promise of action, made concrete by law, that the burden of deficits and debts will be reversed so that they do not add to the taxes of tomorrow. It is further hard proof of our commitment to the fiscal responsibility that is a key foundation for future economic growth for Canada and increased prosperity for all Canadians.
Madam Speaker, I want to conclude by thanking you for the opportunity to address the House on this very important bill, and also to encourage all members of this House to support, not just the bill but the concept that revenue to the government has to be specifically earmarked so that we can reduce the debt-the deficit first and ultimately the debt-of this country, so that our children, my children, your children, do not have a burden to face.

When they, in the future, run for Parliament as undoubtedly they will, they will not find themselves faced with the fact that 35 cents out of every dollar has to be spent on the interest before they even start to look at any other expenditures. That is a burden that we all find, Madam Speaker, and I hope that when all is said and done, we will keep that thought in mind: that the children of the future should not have the burden that we have today.

I am going to try and keep my sense of humour here today; it is the end of the week. However, I cannot believe the charade that is being put before us by this bill.
First of all I want to say there is absolutely no way that this government can possibly understand the way this GST is breaking the morale of this country. There is absolutely no way that this government can understand the fact that the creators of wealth in this country are those people who go out and work hard and, through incentive, create the revenue that allows us to pay down the very debt we are all concerned about.
Conservatives are not the only ones concerning themselves about debt. We concern ourselves with debt as well. Yes, we did leave a debt of $180 billion at the end of 1984, but from 1980 to 1983 we had one of the worst world recessions. From 1984 to 1988 you doubled the debt, so let us not throw daggers at each other on the debt.
Where I have problems with the Conservative government is its total lack of imagination. It thinks the way you eliminate debt is sell off Via Rail, sell off Air Canada, sell off the Royal Canadian Mint, sell, sell, sell. That is the extent of their creativity, one word: sell.
I know this member sits on the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance. He has listened to pleas from all sectors of this economy. My simple question to him is this: at what point in time does he feel that he can stop pushing the morale of this country further down? At what point in time does he feel we should stop doing that, and get back into a more hopeful, wealth creation mode? I do not think he or his party realizes-or at least I am not seeing any demonstration of it-that the pain out there right now, because of the people unemployed, because of the many small businesses that are just hanging on by their fingernails, is being exacerbated by this GST. This debt reduction fund has absolutely nothing to do with reality because the money you receive on the excess GST, if it went into general revenue, still goes against the debt.
The general revenue fund is not some separate institution. It is all part of the same balance sheet of the Government of Canada. Why you are setting up this bogeyman called the debt reduction fund is beyond me. Why could you not use the same kind of creativity to put some job creation plans forward? I am not saying spend more, but let us put our energy back into putting people back to work.
Again, my specific question is, how much more do you really want to push the morale of this country?

Madam Speaker, it is interesting that the member started off and threw a bunch of daggers and then said he would not throw any daggers on the debt, so I will not throw any daggers either.
I would just point out that when the morale of this country was good-and I will acknowledge that-the deficit went. We doubled the debt in the period up to 1977, in two years. We doubled it again three years later and we doubled it again four years after that. Within a period of about eight years, the opposition quadrupled the debt. Perhaps that is even quadrupled. Anyway, it is a big number.
You ask how we are going to change the morale? Well, we are changing the morale because we are making long-term decisions.
The GST is not just an isolated program. There is a number of companies in my riding which were real winners by the GST because we got rid of an unfair manufacturing tax. That is how to start to improve situations in this country. That is how to help those people who create the wealth you were talking about. There is no other way to get out of the dilemma this country faces other than improving the over-all wealth of Canada, the over-all generation of funds through job creation and through investment decisions. It is the GST that has made a lot of those decisions easier. People will be willing to make those decisions and spend the money on GST as long as they can be assured that the money will be targeted against the very thing that you and I have

raised, and that is the debt. This bill guarantees that will happen.
The alternative is we could tell the truckers tomorrow that we will reduce the taxes on their concerns. It is easy to do. It just raises the deficit. Morale would be great, but you know my kids do not want their morale shattered like that.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a brief comment in this debate.
The member from the government side speaks of the deficit of money. I wonder why he neglected to mention a very fundamental deficit and that is the deficit of the people, the poor of our country. To me it is a real deficit. Because of the poverty of over 1 million Canadians, many of our children drop out of school. When they drop out in alarming numbers, they develop no skills to prepare them for the work force.
Does the member not see that preparation of our youth for the work force will guarantee the future of our country, guarantee their employment and guarantee our productivity?
The Senate of Canada recently issued a report and I wonder if the member has read that report on poverty. In it is mentioned very clearly that if we invest $5 billion today, 20 years hence we will have a return of some $28 billion to this country in terms of increased productivity, increased taxes from the revenues that will be generated from these workers, reduced payment to the welfare assistance program because these people will be productive, and so on.
I ask the member what proposal would he have to solve the problem of poverty out of this GST income? I would suggest that for this to proceed, a fund from the GST has to be earmarked for the poor of our country.

Madam Speaker, in my speech I made a comment about people lining up to spend money that was not there and you have just had another example of people lining up wanting money. This money has simply replaced the federal sales tax. So, to this point there is not all this extra money.
The member talks about the deficit of the people and I understand his concern and it is a very legitimate concern. He says there was a report that if we simply threw $5 billion at the problem today, we would get $28 billion back, I believe, in 20 years is what he said. That $5

billion today is $5 billion that is borrowed. Compound interest on that $5 billion over 20 years, I do not know what it would be worth, but it would be a lot more than $28 billion. So it is a net loss.
The point is that we are not short of money in the education system. That point has been made. Canada has one of the highest per capita expenditures on education in the world. Our problem is that we are not educating the students with the money we are putting in the system. Maybe that ought to be reviewed. There are a lot of students coming out of schools who are unable to read or write. How come? How come they can go to school and not come out at the other end with a useful skill? So, I do not think throwing money at it is the solution. Perhaps we have to readdress just how the money is being spent to ensure that we in fact accomplish some of the things that the hon. member is concerned about. Yes, there is a deficit, but simply throwing money at the problem is not the answer.
We have to invest money wisely in job creation. We also have to invest money to ensure that those creators of wealth have the opportunity to multiply their successes to address the very concern that the member has raised.

Madam Speaker, I have just a few words on this bill at second reading stage. Of course, at second reading stage we are debating the principle of the bill.
I presume, after reading the title of the bill, that the principle of the bill is that 7 per cent tax that everyone pays. No matter where they go they cannot avoid that 7 per cent tax. If they go into a store they pay the 7 per cent tax. If they get into a taxi they pay the 7 per cent tax. Why, we even pay it when our life is ending. It is everywhere. The principle of this bill is to take that 7 per cent GST and eliminate the debt of Canada over a period of time.
It strikes me that there is something seriously wrong with that approach if the tax is unevenly distributed throughout Canada. In other words, people in northern Canada or British Columbia or Newfoundland, people at the far extremities of this nation, cannot just go down to the factory or close to a factory and purchase an item. In between the point from which an item is manufactured in Canada and the point at which someone buys it, in

between that space, there is a proliferation of that 7 per cent GST.
In other words, it could be argued that someone who lives in British Columbia pays more into the GST fund than someone who lives where the item that person is buying is manufactured. Someone who lives in northern Canada would also pay more. The item has to be manufactured, trucked to a distributor, taken by the distributor, moved to the retailer and then sold to the individual.
Is it really fair for the government to say that it will retire the debt of Canada by means of the GST and as a result have people in the far extremities of this country shouldering a greater percentage of the national debt on a per capita basis than other people? The actual principle of the bill is faulty.
Living in provinces that already have a high retail sales tax is quite different from living in a province that has no retail sales tax. It started with the telephones. People picked up their telephone bills and saw that the federal government had now gone into retail taxes on long distance telephone calls. They looked at the bill and saw one tax added to the total cost and then another tax, and they were paying double on that tax. It was not just 8 per cent plus 7 per cent to make 15 per cent. It was 8 per cent on the total amount and then 7 per cent on that total amount, which added up not to a 15 per cent tax but a 16 per cent tax and a 17 per cent tax.
When you look at the tax itself, it is unfair because-

The hon. member from Alberta is pointing out that one tax is provincial and the other one is federal. I already said that.
Is it really fair to have a bill like this that says: "Well, all right, we are going to take all the revenues from this and we are going to retire the national debt on that basis."
The ordinary Canadian must be sitting back and saying: "Well, my goodness, if that is going to take care of the national debt then what about all the other things that the Government of Canada brought in which it said were to take care of the national debt?"
The government totally changed the unemployment insurance scheme in this country on the basis that the national debt needed to be serviced and it could no longer afford to contribute to the unemployment insurance scheme. Day after day in this Chamber we listened to the minister saying: "We have got to get out of unemployment insurance because we have got to retire this national debt. We cannot afford to be part of the unemployment insurance scheme any more and we are now going to make it more difficult to get unemployment insurance". It then brought in this outrageous scheme where people now have to figure out which side of the line they live on. If they live on this side of the line they need 13 weeks to qualify, if they live on this side of the line they need 10 weeks to qualify. That was all in the name of retiring the debt. Every public servant was sent these memos saying that they were making a great contribution toward retiring the national debt.
In the case of the unemployment insurance bill-I recall it was C-21 and this one is C-21-the government had a gold button it sent to all the public servants, or gold plated I suppose but not really gold, saying C-21. Everybody got it this past year. Lo and behold, open up the button and it says: "Made in the U.S.A.". It sent them mugs that said: "Working together for the retirement of the debt". If you turned over the mug it said: "Made in Thiwan".
We have listened to the government say: "We are going to retire the debt, get rid of the debt and that is why we changed the unemployment insurance scheme". The government even removed the railway tracks in some provinces on the basis that it could not keep making those expenditures because the national debt was too high. It discontinued the railway services. We can no longer go to North Sydney, Nova Scotia by railway because that service has been discontinued from Truro. In Newfoundland there is no more freight service at all and practically all the tracks are up now. I think the tracks are being sent to somewhere in Venezuela. The
September 20, 1991

railway ties are being piled up but they are not much good. It left a big roadway across the province. I only wish Newfoundland had made a settlement with the Government of Canada to pave them or something so at least it could be used instead of just having some crushed stone there.
All of this was done in the name of the national debt.
Madam Speaker, I can recall them standing in this Chamber and saying that they must now impose great restrictions on our postal service because of the national debt. That was the rationale.
Canadians would turn around now after hearing about this bill and say: "Oh, does this mean we are going to get back our post office now because we lost it because there needed to be payments into the treasury because of the national debt". They lost their post office because of the national debt.
It takes two weeks on average for a letter to be sent from point A to point B in this country because of the national debt. I know members of Parliament get these surveys all the time conducted by learned consulting groups and accounting firms that say: "The service is great." That is only if the letter is addressed and typewritten, put out by a computer and the address is directly in the centre of the envelope. Not if one sits down and writes the address.
Every member of Parliament is being phoned by students saying that their student loans have not been approved although the notification has been sent to the university. As one knows, students go and pick up their student loans at the university. Notification has been sent, but it has not arrived there yet. It was sent out two weeks ago. So and so wrote a letter to her granddaughter last Christmas some time and it arrived just the other day. All of this was done in the name of the national debt.
The transfer payments to provinces for health and education were cut in the budget because of the national debt. Does this mean now that the Government of Canada is going to turn around and reinstate the transfer payments to the provinces for health and education, for

the running of our hospitals, for equipment in our hospitals? Hospitals today are under this incredible squeeze, all by provincial governments, because the provincial governments were cut back by the federal government in the name of retiring the debt.
Every budget speech, if one goes back over and looks at them every year, and that was the rationale. There was no other rationale. It said: "We have to cut down on transfer payments to provincial governments for hospitals, health and post-secondary education. Why? Because of the national debt. It was not because of anything else. That was it. That is all.
Does this mean now with this 7 per cent of everything in this country, when an individual walks into a store anywhere, he or she pays 7 per cent and all this money goes into the retiring of the debt? And this is going to retire the debt, this is what is needed to retire the debt?
Does this mean now that the federal government-it would make sense- would turn around and reverse what it did in the previous budget, which was to state that in order to retire the debt, it had to reduce the payments for health and post-secondary education in the provinces?
It is one or the other. Either this is going to reduce the debt, or it is not going to reduce the debt. Either this is the sole means of doing it, or all of these other things have to be done as well to do it. The question is: What is it? Why is the Government of Canada behaving every single day like some massive tax grabber?
Madam Speaker, here is a good one for you. You will be interested in this, coming from Montreal, Quebec. I obtained a copy of a proposed new cost recovery policy. Why is it there? It is there because the federal government continues to say day after day, month after month, to the Public Service of this country: "Look, you've got to find ways of raising more money. We want you to collect more money. We want you to cut back."
The federal government brought in a scheme three years ago to give a manager in the Public Service a bonus if he could find ways of collecting new taxes, to give him as bonus if he could get rid of more people. They called it a productivity bonus. In other words, if you cut down on the numbers of employees under you then you received a cash bonus before Christmas, a productivity bonus. It was

Now here is a good one for you, Madam Speaker. This one was just the other day. Here is the statement: "Earmarked taxes," which is what this is in this bill, "could take the form of a charge on commercial carriers or on shippers in relation to the value of the cargo, or to the water transport charge, or a charge based on fuel purchased."
Of course what this is is a discussion paper, a proposed new cost recoveiy policy for the Department of Transport. The authority to do that was found under the Aeronautics Act. It is quite simple.
Beyond that authority one finds in individual acts the Government of Canada was stymied, it did not know how it could extend that principle which was contained in certain pieces of legislation to a broader spectrum to allow government departments and civil servants in managerial positions to be able to come up with ideas to have more taxes, to earmark more taxes for specific reasons. It found the solution in this session of Parliament and it went through this House in the Financial Administration Act, and members who were on the finance committee would know what I am talking about. The Financial Administration Act was changed to encourage and to allow government departments to seek ways of raising new taxes within their department.
Here is one of them. Now what is this? What does it mean? What it means is that the federal government is now going to have an earmarked tax on buoys. On buoys. Not on men or women, but buoys. These are buoys. Of course I looked it up and it said they do not call them buoys, they call them floating navigational aids. They say here, here's a brilliant statement: "In many parts of Canada most floating navigational aids are removed during the winter." A very intelligent statement, especially when the ice is around. A continuing "nav-aids" charge would still be justified because non-floating
Well, it is kind of difficult when there is ice for a hundred miles. How does one navigate over ice or under ice for 200 miles? One is still going to be charged for it. Yes, one is still going to be charged.
I notice you telling me two minutes, Madam Speaker. I have not even got to the point of the bill that I was going to talk about but I will continue with this point. The federal government is in this psychology of earmarking taxes, of having government departments devise means of taxing people.
Here is one here that says it is now going to make a charge on cargo. Here is the suggestion to the government. I do not know whether it is going to do it. Some of the companies think it is going to do it. Companies right across Canada were sent letters by the government saying it was going to do it. It is going to tax you for using buoys in the water, so much per nautical mile.
It comes from this order by the federal government that you have to tax everything. You have to collect more money to pay for this, pay for that, pay for something else.

speechtext:
Yes, incestuous, but I will not go into it in this Elouse. I will be apologizing later.
It is a great pleasure as usual to follow my friend and colleague and countryman, the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls. I had the privilege just last week to be driving on the Trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland. As I came up the hill out of Benton, it was very confusing all of a sudden. It was mid-day. I thought for a second I was in the middle of the big runway at the international airport in Gander. Here was blacktop, pavement, six lanes of pavement. I did not know where it had come from. It had no lines on it. I did not know which was the passing lane, which was the new shoulder. We do not have shoulders on the paved roads in Newfoundland much. But now we do. All we have are little yellow dots down the road. As sometimes is the case, some people were driving a little quickly. There was an RCMP officer coming and we all slowed down and I had the opportunity to look. There is nothing but pavement.
Do you know what the big issue is today in the town of Gander? The bypass. Where are we going to put the road: through or around Gander? But, Madam Speaker, as you know, except at certain times every four years in Newfoundland, pavement just does not arrive from nowhere. Pavement is paid for. It is very expensive. We are talking over $1 million a mile. That is for what we are used to, which is two lanes, but now we are going four lanes right across the province. All through my constituency it is four lanes. Into Gander it is four lanes.
You should see what they are doing in Corner Brook with bypasses and overpasses and underpasses. Do you know where that is coming from Madam Speaker? That is coming from the $800 million that this government was able to pay to the province of Newfoundland and Labrador: "Let us sign an agreement. The railway is not being used, it is a disincentive to industry, it is a disincentive to transportation. Let us build the roads that are essential through this province so that we have half a chance to transport goods around the province."
Very quickly if I may, Madam Speaker, on this GST. We are talking about cuts in the government. This government has not cut 2,500 jobs out of its Public Service, just like that. Like the Government of New-
Government Orders
foundland and Labrador has done, just like that. Just like that, 2,500 jobs gone this year. And what, in the name of good financial and fiscal management?
Wage freezes. We live in a small society in Newfoundland and Labrador. We tend to know each other. We have neighbours, we have friends, we have relatives that come and go in our lives in politics and in business and that sort of thing. That gives us an opportunity to speak to these people, people that we went to school with, our cousins, perhaps our brothers even. It gives us the opportunity to pass messages along.
If my brother were the President of the Treasury Board in Newfoundland and Labrador, I would tell him first of all that he should not cut these jobs, he should not close six hospitals, he should not close technical schools. The last thing I would tell my brother if he were President of the Treasury Board is that I would not take the goods and services tax and harmonize it with the provincial sales tax, as is happening in Newfoundland and Labrador. But my brother is not the President of the Treasury Board.

subtopic: DEBT SERVICING AND REDUCTION ACCOUNT ACT

I thought the hon. member heard me when I said that I was not my brother's speaker. But I might remind the hon. member that when he referred to Benton, the community of Benton is just outside of Gander, and he is correct, it is on the Trans-Canada Highway. I must admit when you do go up over the hill, you are confronted by all of this blacktop. Now, in Newfoundland when you have got good pavement that is what you call it, and everybody just looks forward to having paved roads. I mean, there are parts of my federal riding that have these dirty rotten dirt roads and you are down to the crank case in mud in the spring and you cannot move, and this sort of thing.
But I must admit that when you come up over that hill in Benton and you see all of that beautiful new pavement, well there is a reason for that. That is the beginning of the riding of that great Liberal member who called the tenders and his name happens to be Winston Baker.

Madam Speaker, I would like to get back to the bill. It is all very well for us to have an historical accounting of how they build roads in Newfoundland, but I want to ask my friend and colleague about the bill.

September 20, 1991
The annual deficit is the object here of this initiative. I want to ask the member, if he really believes this is nothing but smoke and mirrors on the government's part, in his opinion will this change the debt position of the government in any way? Will this create any new income? Will it bring in new revenues? Will it prevent it from spending further than it has spent, like it announced today, or yesterday? Rather, they are moving 200 public servants from the riding of Ottawa-Vanier to Regina. Welcome: "Oink, oink, oink," as Jeffrey Simpson says this morning. Welcome again to Brian Mulro-ney's Ottawa.
Ladies and gentlemen, you haven't learned anything yet. It moved 200 public servants to Regina and it found $236 million for the so-called TRIUMF KAON particle accelerator.
I just wonder if the member could comment briefly on how this bill is going to prevent this government from going: "oink, oink, oink," come every election time.

Madam Speaker, I must admit, and people looking at this must think it is quite a coincidence, all of a sudden for the Government of Canada to find all of this money to develop an industry that has been demanded in British Columbia for years. The scientists out there have been demanding it. They have been demanding it year after year after year after year to create those jobs. All of a sudden, what a coincidence. The day the election is called out there, yes, the very minister who used to be in the cabinet out there with that government goes down and announces that particular expenditure.
Meanwhile back in the hon. member's riding now, what do they have? They have all of the employees there being offered zero per cent wage increases. And all at the same time, we have 4,600 of the upper management people getting their bonuses. So that is the Government of Canada's way, it is entirely political, and I am sure that all we can look forward to for the next two years are political announcements, loads of money to spend, because they have taxed everybody to death.

The purpose is to promote the vaccination of high-risk groups, and I am sure you will agree, from personal experience, Madam Speaker. People at risk are usually those over 65 and and those suffering from chronic illness such as asthma, heart disease or diabetes.
These people should get a flu vaccination to protect themselves against infection and avoid often serious complications. speechtext: Unfortunately, the hon. member's time is up, but I would like to thank him for his excellent advice.

Madam Speaker, on Tbesday on behalf of the Liberal Party, I called on the Prime Minister to support the ceasefire in Yugoslavia, and to act on the request by the presidents of Yugoslavia and Croatia for peacekeepers from the United Nations. I congratulate him on the speed with which he acted on our suggestion.
I trust, however, that Ambassador Fortier will do more than just inform the United Nations Security Council and the European Community. Canada's position, in light of the new internationalism, must be to place individual and minority human rights above the absolute rights of sovereign states.
September 20,1991

I met yesterday with representatives of the Canadian Croatian Information Centre. These Canadians, many of whom are sitting in the gallery right now, know it is possible for all people to live in harmony when there is true democracy. One woman said: "This war should not been seen as Serbs against Croatians. It is democracy against communism".
If true democracy is to prevail, the UN must act now.

Madam Speaker, two days ago in this House the hon. member for Hamilton West quoted some of my words to the press. It was his intent to demonstrate that I did not agree with the Minister of Finance that the recession is over.
This was a highly partisan attempt to gain a few political points, and the member ought to be ashamed of himself. As usual he was ill-informed and misinterpreted my statement.
As both he and I know, leading economic indicators show the recession is clearly over. Unemployment figures also show that it will take some time before all of the lost jobs are regained. Until those jobs come back, neither of us I am sure, will be satisfied.
I have no hesitation in saying that the policies of the Minister of Finance, including spending restraint, falling interest rates, low inflation and deficit reduction are the very reasons those jobs will be regained and will be permanent.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the closure of the Lingan mine in my constituency of Cape Breton-East Richmond will undoubtedly have a negative effect on our economy, an economy that is already hurting.
On previous occasions in this House I have warned both the federal and provincial governments that the opening of the Westray coal mine in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, would mean in effect the closure of the Lingan mine in Cape Breton.
On several occasions, both in Question Period as well as statements, I have brought this to the attention of the Prime Minister. I am supported by senior management
of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, a federal Crown corporation, which has supplied information to the Government of Canada that if the Westray coal mine proceeded, Lingan would have to close.
Details of the compensation package which was worked out between union and management for the displaced workers at Lingan has yet to be announced. I insist that the president and the board of directors of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, as well as the minister, honour their commitment and provide the details of that compensation package immediately and not waste any more time in providing those answers.

Madam Speaker, for over 124 years, Canada has been closely linked by interprovincial trade. Six provinces; Quebec, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta trade more within Canada than they export to foreign countries.
Of the three largest manufacturing provinces, only Quebec is more dependent on trade with other Canadian provinces than on foreign trade. Quebec's manufacturing shipments are roughly split between international markets and the rest of Canada. In 1989, 14.5 per cent of Quebec's shipments of manufactured goods went to Ontario. Only 5.9 per cent of Ontario's went to Quebec.
Interprovincial trade is vitally important to all provinces. If Canada breaks up and trade flows are disrupted, each and every one of us would personally be worse off than we are today.

Madam Speaker, the co-chair of the International Joint Commission Science Advisory Board has called for a declaration that chemical contaminants in the Great Lakes are a hazard to human health.
Some 37 million Canadians and Americans are facing health threats ranging from infertility to birth defects from the toxic wastes dumped into the five lake system. This adds to the urgent IJC call for an outright ban on the 11 most persistent toxics and demonstrates once again the need for a zero discharge timetable, solemnly

promised by the Prime Minister four years ago. Further delay would be criminal.
On Wednesday, the minister of energy attempted to abandon Canada's commitment on global warming. He said, and I quote: "It is Canada's policy to stabilize greenhouse gas emissions by the year 2000".
On November 7, 1990 in Geneva the Minister of the Environment stated, and I quote: "Canada has pledged to fully eliminate controlled CFCs by 1997. We have also committed, as a minimum, to stabilize at 1990 levels all other greenhouse gases, most notably carbon dioxide, by the year 2000".
Let us trust that Canada did not lie in Geneva.

Madam Speaker, I applaud the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture that FCC headquarters will at long last move to the prairies.
The bulk of farm credit business is on the prairies. The base of Saskatchewan is agriculture. The move makes sense. However, it will come as no surprise to westerners that the opposition parties are bellyaching about this long overdue decision.
The Liberals call it a crass effort to buy votes. What hypocrisy. Ottawa Liberal members should stop toadying to Daryl Bean long enough to understand that a considerable part of Canada lies beyond the lush pastures of the national capital region.
The NDP are no better. They have 10 members from Saskatchewan who should be elated about this relocation. But no, they are so tied to the apron strings of the Public Service Alliance and the big Ontario union bosses that they are forced to do what they do best, criticize, find fault and be negative.
I congratulate the Minister of Agriculture on this relocation, which demonstrates the continuing commitment of this government to bring federal institutions and agencies close to the people they serve.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the economic recession has again hit the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. Yesterday, St. Isidore Meats Inc., the only pork abattoir between Toronto and Montreal, announced it was closing, laying off its last forty employees. A few months ago, thirty more people lost their jobs in St. Isidore.
Madam Speaker, it seems that every week another disaster strikes the people of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and eastern Ontario. This morning, I would again like to tell the government opposite that my colleagues from Stormont-Dundas and Renfrew-Nipissing- Pembroke, I and twenty-eight municipalities of eastern Ontario asked the government to act and set up a development program for our region. We need it now.

Madam Speaker, the Mulroney government is literally draining the national capital with its decentralization policy, which I have decried many times. After the move of the National Energy Board to Calgary in July, the national capital is now dealt another blow with the announcement of the transfer of the head office of the Farm Credit Corporation from Ottawa to Regina. Quebecers will have no alternative but to leave Quebec to pursue their career in Saskatchewan. Since the constitutional offers are about to be presented, we can expect this haemorrhage to intensify and in the worst case, gifts to be given across Canada to help the "pill" go down. The decentralization of thousands of jobs has very serious consequences for the Quebec side of the Ottawa River. It is high time that Quebec took back all its powers and became sovereign.
September 20, 1991

Madam Speaker, women are marching this weekend in cities across the country to take back the night. Shelters for battered women are unfunded. Women's sexual histories are on trial once again.
An all-party report of the House of Commons subcommittee on the status of women called for a strong rape shield law, adequate funding for shelters and crisis centres, mandatory gender sensitivity training for judges and members of Parliament. The need has never been more evident.
Recent events here have shown Canadians the type of behaviour that is sometimes directed at women members of Parliament. It is not hard to see why there is no pay equity when a government representative, responsible for pay equity, makes offensive comments about women.
New Democrats call upon this government to implement the recommendations of that report now.

Madam Speaker, this week saw 15 innocent people charged and summoned to appear in criminal court. Among them was the Commissioner of the RCMP and two members of the force.

These charges resulted from private prosecutions under section 507 of the Criminal Code. This section allows a justice of the peace, who sometimes has no legal training, to determine if a summons should be issued. It should be changed to require a judge or a Crown attorney to review the evidence and charges before they are continued.
Fifteen people spent an intolerable summer with their reputations tarnished because of the media's misunderstanding of private prosecutions and the vengeful mind of one person. It even hurt our entire country by causing an unwarranted run on our dollar.
This misuse of our justice system should not be allowed to happen to any citizen of our country again.

Madam Speaker, the city of Cornwall and other communities in eastern Ontario need a federal economic development program now.
Federal programs such as FEDNOR and the Canada-Quebec Subsidiary Agreement have proved to be beneficial to northern Ontario and particular regions of Quebec. A similar program is required for economically depressed areas in eastern Ontario.
Unemployment is well above the national average in Cornwall, where over 1,500 lay-offs and job losses have occurred in the last two years. The absence of an economic development program has inhibited businesses and investment from locating in eastern Ontario.
The negative impact of cross-border shopping and the geographic reality has eastern Ontario up against northern New York state and western Quebec in attracting business and investors. This places border communities like Cornwall at a distinct disadvantage.
Cornwall, and cities like Pembroke and Hawkesbury, need an federal economic development from this government immediately.

Madam Speaker, the Conservative government continues to attack the Ontario government for its budget deficit and, at the same time, faces a situation where its own deficit is rising far faster than it projected in the budget last year.
The latest figures show that for the first four months of this fiscal year, the budget deficit that the Conservative government is running is twice as high as the budget deficit which it ran last year. At that rate we are looking at a potential budget deficit of over $35 billion.
This is not something this government can use as ammunition if it seeks to show the rest of the country that fiscal rectitude is an important consideration.

September 20, 1991
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, an extraordinary event will take place next year when more than 100 world leaders will meet at an earth summit in Rio de Janiero. We will be discussing preservation of the ecological integrity of the planet. We will also be discussing the integration of the environment and the economy in both developed and developing countries, and the need for a partnership between north and south.
The earth summit is officially called the United Nations Conference on the Environment and Development. It will take place in Rio de Janiero June 1 to 12,
1992.
The Government of Canada is actively preparing for the conference in concert with partners in the provinces and the territories, in industry, in environmental and development groups. We are working with our aboriginal people, Canadian youth, women's groups, religious and peace organizations, scientists and academics, all of whom are part of the Canadian team. The delegation has requested that this example be emulated at the international level.

Madam Speaker, Canadians reeled in shock this past summer at the tragic deaths of several young Canadians. In southern Ontario two young women, Leslie Mahaffy and Nina DeVilliers, and a child, Kala Klaudusz, met violent and needless deaths.
Canadians have expressed shock and horror at these incidents and are asking themselves where is the justice. People see the perpetrators of violent crimes released prematurely from jail, violent offenders are walking the streets on day passes.
Canadians are asking themselves: "Why is our justice system working against us? How can we be protected against violent offenders today and in the future?" Both society at large and the victims of violence are demanding that justice be done. We must remember to put a face to these tragedies.
During this fall session I will table a private member's bill dealing with the rights of victims of violence. It will give the victims of violence a stronger voice in the
disposition of convicted offenders and will return to society a sense of security and faith in their system of justice.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The government says that the recession is over, but the economic indicators say otherwise. Manufacturers' deliveries are down. The trade surplus is at its lowest level in ten years, and unemployment continues to increase. When will the government at least admit that its policies are harming the Canadian economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, quite the contrary. The hon. member knows there was substantial growth recorded in the second quarter. The budget projections of February 1991 assumed that recovery would start occurring in the second half. Recovery has actually started one quarter earlier than that which was projected and it was at a very robust level of 4.9 per cent on an annualized basis.
We projected all along that the recovery would be modest to moderate and we projected growth in the order of 3.1 per cent in 1992. We now anticipate that growth will be something in the order of 2.5 per cent to 3 per cent in the second half.
Export volumes have increased by over 25 per cent at an annual rate in the second quarter. Business confidence is up. Consumer confidence is up. Housing starts are up. Housing sales are up. All of these are positive indicators that lead me to believe that we are on the road to a sustainable moderate recovery.

Madam Speaker, yesterday the Canadian dollar closed at 88.09 cents. Will the Minister of Finance give to this House the name of just one Canadian industrialist who has come up to him and said: "Thank you, Minister. Your high-dollar policy is really helping us to compete and to create jobs in Canada".
September 20, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is intelligent enough to know that you cannot artificially manipulate the value of the dollar. There are market forces at play that contribute to the value of the dollar, and I remind him that notwithstanding the fact that interest rates have declined by over 5.5 per cent, or 550 basis points, from last year, the spread has declined from about 565 basis points to 280 basis points.
Notwithstanding that fact, when we had the high spreads and the high interest rates the dollar was worth 84 cents. Interest rates have come down. The value of the dollar has gone up.
This tells us that there is confidence in the Canadian economy and strength in the integrity of the Canadian dollar. That should be applauded and not be criticized.

Madam Speaker, for this minister to support his high dollar policy is totally wrong.
Labour does not like it. Small business does not like it. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association said: "It is putting Canadian manufacturers out of business and their employees out of work." Who is wrong, Canadians or this government?
Will this government reverse its high dollar policy to help resuscitate Canadian industry and get Canadians back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one of the contributing factors to the upward pressure on the dollar is the fact that the provinces have been borrowing very extensively in the international marketplace.
As a matter of fact, in the first half of this year, they have borrowed $10.9 billion in new debt issues. That is double the amount of the whole year of 1990. That puts upward pressure on the dollar.
The other fact is that North America is a safe haven for investment when there is uncertainty throughout the world, and that is another contributing factor.
I remind the hon. member that the President of the National Bank, Andre Berard, as reported in Le Devoir as reported this morning, said that reducing producing
Oral Questions
production costs is just as important to economic recovery as readjusting to the high value of the Canadian dollar.
It is not just the value of the dollar that is contributing to our difficulties. It is production costs. It is labour efficiency. It is labour cost components. Those are the things that we must address together.
My colleague, the Minister for International Trade, will be unveiling a strategy to improve our competitiveness and our prosperity. That is a positive sign.

Madam Speaker, I also have a question for the Minister of Finance.
Yesterday, the head of the second largest newsprint manufacturer in the world, Hugh Fletcher, speaking in Toronto said: "The difference between an 88-cent dollar and an 80-cent dollar is the difference between disaster and reasonableness."
Why is this government running an economic policy that international business leaders who have to make decisions about investing in Canada are calling a disaster? That does not sound like confidence to me.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, these same business leaders were complaining about high interest costs a year ago.
Interest rates have come down by 5.5 per cent. They are still coming down. The Bank of Montreal announced that its prime rate would be 9.25 per cent. That certainly is a far cry from the 22.75 per cent when that minister sat over here on the treasury benches.

Madam Speaker, Canadians watching will note that the Minister of Finance neglected to respond in any way to the comments of Mr. Hugh Fletcher, international business leader and head of the second largest newsprint manufacturing company in the world.
Mr. Fletcher also said, speaking of the monetary policy, the high dollar policy of this government, that the Governor of the Bank of Canada is "killing prospects" of international investors putting more money into our crucial forest products sector.
Why is this government acting to kill prospects of international investment in the forest products sector if it is interested in international confidence and business

September 20, 1991
Oral Questions
leaders like Mr. Fletcher investing in Canada? Why does it not reverse its harmful economic policies right now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps I should remind the hon. member and Mr. Fletcher that the average value of the Canadian dollar over the last 40 years was 92.6 cents.
When he talks about the value of the high dollar, on a historical basis he is right out of kilter on this thing. The fact of the matter is that the dollar, as he knows, is set in the marketplace. There is intervention by the Bank of Canada to ensure that there are not erratic ups and downs in the level of the interest rates. It is the marketplace that establishes the rate.
In so far as investment, there has been a turnaround of about $7 billion since the free trade agreement came in. Before the free trade, there was a net outflow of investment dollars. As a result of the free trade, the investment policies and the confidence that business has in this government, there has been a net inflow of investment dollars.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday, we again heard that nearly one-third of single parent families live in poverty. One child out of five lives in poverty. Here is my question. We are about to debate the future of our country, and during this debate, we cannot afford to ignore these frightening figures because these children are our future. For many years, this government has failed to take any new measures to deal with a disastrous situation. What is the government going to do, not in a couple of years but now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
As I indicated yesterday, Madam Speaker, this government has initiated a number of programs that has improved the situation of children. I agree with the hon. member that children and the family unit are basic to our society. We have attempted through
tax reform to try to improve the lot of families, in particular with respect to children.
I also want to remind the hon. member that since we have come to office, more than 1 million people have been taken off the poverty roll, which includes over
300,000	children. The changes to the child tax credit and the various tax credits that have been provided to lower and middle income people and the refund of the GST tax credit, all of these things are in recognition of the very important fact of family life, and particularly those families who live on lower and middle incomes.
Always we wish that we could do more. The minister of health is currently looking at a number of child initiatives which are being developed. When they are developed, they will be announced in the House in the appropriate fashion.

Madam Speaker, this government has been in power since 1984. It is time to stop wishing and put in some initiatives for these children.
On November 24, 1989, this House unanimously-including the Deputy Prime Minister, the Minister Responsible for the Constitution and the Prime Minister-voted unanimously to make a commitment to eradicate child poverty by the year 2000.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister: As well as the initiatives that absolutely need to be taken now, and as we move into the constitutional debate, is the government seriously considering a social charter which would give specificity to these fine words that were uttered in 1989, two years ago, to really address the basic issues that will unite this country?
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister: Will his government seriously consider a social charter which will include the right of children to have a decent standard of living and to have food and shelter and education in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one of the best ways that we can improve the lot and the confidence of children and future generations is to deal more effectively with the burden of debt which has been inherited by this government and which this government is trying to deal with without very much support from the New Democratic Party.
*g*

September 20, 1991

In so far as her question about a social charter, the hon. member will have access to the document next week. It will be presented in the House. It will be debated. I am sure that the hon. member will have an expressed point of view at that particular time.
As the Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs has stated on many occasions and as the Prime Minister has stated, this is a beginning and not an end. What the government is proposing is an advancement of proposals which we hope will find favour and we hope the hon. member and her party will engage in a further discussion to develop the kinds of programs and policies that will lead us to the kind of Canada that we all aspire to achieve in terms of a strong economy, a sensitivity to social concerns, but most important, a strong political unit.

My supplementary question is for the Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs. Canadians are very concerned that our health care is in jeopardy, there is no child care program, that poverty still exists in this country despite the words that we have said in this House.
Clearly we all agree that this country needs a shared commitment to making Canada the best place possible. I want ask the minister: Is he seriously considering, and will he consider in principle, that a social charter would give form and substance to those sentiments, and is he considering that now?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one of the advantages of having specific propositions on the table, as there will be next Tuesday, is that some of the concerns that might have been raised about the contents of the proposals of the government will be allayed, will be answered by the publication of the specific document.
The hon. member will know that Premier Rae, in Ontario, who I understand is planning to publish a document with respect to a charter, had at one point been interested in bringing forward and devising a charter itself. His officials, as I understand it, encountered some difficulty in translating that interesting idea
Oral Questions
into a charter that would work and would be acceptable within the Canadian system.
I want to repeat what the Deputy Prime Minister has just said, that the proposals that we put forward on Thesday are proposals that will be considered, that are designed to achieve real change in the Constitution, that are firm but that are not final. If it is the view of members of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution that there needs to be improvements brought to that package, certainly we will look with an open mind on all practical improvements.
I emphasize that we are interested in improvements, things that will work, not simply proposals for change.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for Science.
For the past seven years, members of this government have told Canadians time and again that there is no money for the National Research Council, no money for industrial research, no money for medical and environmental research.
My question to the minister is: Where has the government suddenly found the money to fund the KAON project?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the member knows, in the last budget of February there was $1.5 billion set aside for science and technology initiatives in this next several years. That funding is still in place and has nothing whatsoever to do with the KAON project.
KAON project funding, as far as the Government of Canada is concerned, would come in in later years and that funding is not at all a part of the $1.5 billion.

Madam Speaker, I am glad that the government has suddenly found a rich uncle. I would like to tell the minister that the line starts right here.
Is the minister saying that the government has now found money to support adequately university research, industrial research, medical and environmental research, or is this just pure political opportunism?

September 20, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think it would be just as well if the hon. member would wait until he sees the proposals for spending the $1.5 billion.
Furthermore, I think it would be just as well if he waited until the consultations with respect to prosperity and competitiveness are over, until we see what further funding may be needed to do some of the things he has on his plate.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture.
The news that the Farm Credit Corporation headquarters is being relocated to Regina has sent shock waves rippling through more than 200 families of public servants in the national capital region.
My question is: Why is the government fuelling public cynicism by announcing this move on the eve of a provincial election, and where is the immediate real support for which farmers are asking?

Madam Speaker, I want to inform the hon. member that the most valued resource that the Farm Credit Corporation has are the employees of Farm Credit Corporation.
The move and the relocation of some 200 headquarters staff to Regina will take place over the next 12 months. We hope it is concluded prior to the crop year.
The NDP seems to object to putting 200 jobs into the province of Saskatchewan, locating Farm Credit Corporation where 60 per cent of the clients that Farm Credit serve reside, where over 50 per cent of the dollars are lent out by Farm Credit Corporation. I do not understand why the NDP objects to it so much.

Madam Speaker, as we know the Farm Credit Corporation runs on a non-deficit basis. The minister also knows that the cost of the move and future expenses will be borne by the farmers through higher interest rates. Clearly, the relocation is of no benefit to the farmers whatsoever.
So I repeat my question and ask the minister to answer me and not the NDP. Why is this government using public servants to interfere in provincial elections?

Madam Speaker, as the hon. member knows and as eveiyone in the House knows, the policy of this government is to locate the services that the government provides closest to those clients the department serves.
I draw to the hon. member's attention the relocation a of the National Energy Board to Calgary.
I draw to the hon. member's attention for the same rationale that over 60 per cent of the client group served by Farm Credit reside in the prairie provinces. More than 50 per cent of the dollars lent out by Farm Credit are in the prairie provinces. That will bring the Farm Credit Corporation and its headquarters staff closer to producers.
I say to the hon. member that he has recognized that Farm Credit operates on a break even basis or operates on a basis of no cost to the taxpayer. It also operates on a competitive interest rate policy. Its interest rates are competitive with any commercial institution in Canada.
The savings that will be acquired over the life of the corporation, as they are amortized over the life of the corporation for this move, will be consumed within the corporation and will benefit the farmers and the clients of Farm Credit.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister responding for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
In April Surgitex withdrew the Meme breast implant from the market.
On June 5, Carol Cyr was implanted with two Memes in a hospital in Montreal.
My question to the minister is: How could this happen? Is the Meme off the market or is it not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member has indicated, the Meme breast implant was recalled and to my knowledge it is off the market.

September 20, 1991

Madam Speaker, the hon. minister should know that in fact the Meme has never been recalled by this government. It was withdrawn voluntarily by Surgitex.
On August 7, in a press release the minister said the Meme implant is not currently available and cannot be reintroduced until evidence is reviewed by Health and Welfare.
On September 5, the director of the minister's Bureau of Medical Devices said on CBOFT Radio when asked about Carol Cyr: "It is in no way the business of the federal department of health and welfare".
Could the minister tell this House just who is responsible?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Again, Madam Speaker, some of the statements made by the hon. member are correct. It is off the market. The minister of health has ordered his department to look into this issue again, as it has been raised on a number of occasions and it is of concern not only to the department but to all women in Canada.
With respect to whether or not a doctor proceeded after the recall, doctors were informed of the recall of the Meme breast implant. If a doctor did go ahead with such an operation, I would suggest that the person in question contact the appropriate medical college in order to file a complaint.

Madam Speaker, Canadians are awaiting the announcement next Tuesday of the proposed changes to the Canadian Constitution. From what we hear so far, the west will get an elected Senate, Quebec will get distinct status, and aboriginal people will get self-government.
My question is to the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs. Will middle-class Canadians also get something they deserve: the entrenched right to own
Oral Questions
private property, including the right not to be deprived of that property without just compensation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I very much hope and believe that all Canadians can receive from this package and this process a country that is united and prosperous and that will be able to look to the future, turning all of our attention to means by which we can grow stronger and more prosperous without diversion of constant constitutional problems.
With regard to the specific question respecting property rights, I appreciate the strong representation that has been made by the member and by others in this House.
I cannot divulge the contents of the package until it is released by the Prime Minister on Ihesday, but I can tell the hon. member that the concern raised by him and by hon. members has been taken seriously by this government.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade in the absence of the energy minister, and it relates to the announced $315 million Cemavoda nuclear power station in Romania.
A report of the International Atomic Energy Agency last week indicated that fully a quarter of the station's safety problems has not been dealt with by the present government in Bucharest.
It would also strongly appear that the management of the Export Development Corporation is privately very hostile to this proposed loan.
Will the minister deal with both of those issues please?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there has been a report by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
In this report it has noted a significant degree of progress from this time a year ago when it set out its

September 20, 1991
Oral Questions
proposals as to what should be done to put the Cemavo-da proposal in a position that it could be actively pursued.
We have followed this carefully. We believe that there is still further progress that must be made, but it is on this basis that we have moved forward with the financing from the Export Development Corporation in order to allow the proposal to be completed.
With regard to the second part of the hon. member's question, I am not aware of any opposition.

Madam Speaker, the Iliescu government in Romania continues to inflict what are most often considered to be anti-democratic and authoritarian measures against many of its citizens.
What guarantees has the minister received that once the Atomic Energy Commission of Canada's management contract expires that the government there will continue to show concern for both the safety and human rights of the Romanian people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Tbade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I indicated, the international agency has observed some improvements in things in Romania.
It is a question of human rights that the hon. member has raised. This is something that has been a concern of the federal government. We will continue to make representations in that regard to the government.
As my hon. friend knows, there can be no guarantees in the future. However, what we can be sure of is that since this particular project will be very supportive of improving the standard of living of people in that country, and improving the standard of living almost inevitably leads to fewer excesses in the area of human rights difficulties, we are confident that that will take place in this regard as well.

speechtext:

The 1991 economic rendez-vous organized by the Conseil du patronat du Quebec this week generated 48 job-creation projects, since no action plans were forthcoming from the Tory government.

To help Montreal's economy back on its feet, we included in our February Budget a number of measures to reduce the deficit, bring down inflation and reduce unemployment. That is what we did. September 20, 1991

we do something for Montreal, the hon. member says no!
