Madam Speaker, some months ago Canadians and Parliament welcomed Nelson Mandela to speak of change in South Africa to the Canadian Parliament and people.
This week Canadians are learning from his deputy, and for 26 years his fellow prisoner, Walter Sisulu and his wife Albertina, about the progress and the change toward democracy and the development needs of the future of South Africa.
I know that members will join in welcoming them here in the House today and on their tour of Canada.
I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Last week the Commonwealth committee, which she chairs, spoke of resource needs and the Commonwealth meeting it.
What will Canada do to contribute to the resource needs of a democratic South Africa?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think all members of the House can be proud of Canada's role in fighting apartheid for many, many years. I think that the changes that have been made in recent months and recent years, thanks to outside pressure as well as support for the democratic forces inside South Africa, have been an important factor.
This year, Canada will be providing $15 million in aid specifically for human resource development and education and other aspects of that issue. While I was in Delhi, I announced that we would be giving $1.5 million to the UN High Commission for Refugees to help the political exiles whom we can all help to celebrate on their return home. We will be helping with their resettlement.
There is no country more pleased than Canada about the progress that has been made, but we continue to look to further sanctions to continue the pressure until full democracy reigns in South Africa.

Madam Speaker, yesterday in the House, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development said that all aboriginal students in Canada can have access to a post-secondary education under the program that has been put in place by this government.
I cannot say that the minister deceived the House, but the communications branch damage control strategy from his own ministry, which the minister cited from memory in many parts, indicates that as many as 3,000 students will be unfunded this year. That is 3,000 potential students who, rather than going to school, will end up on social assistance which costs the government roughly 10 per cent less than a post-secondary school education.
Bands and tribal councils, including Squamish, Nanaimo and other bands in the minister's riding, have been handed actual budget cuts by his department this year, contrary to the minister's assurance yesterday and the Prime Minister's promise in Victoria.

Pathways to Excellence Program, there is no excuse for a post-secondary student and young Indian-

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State.
A student from Winnipeg called me today, one of over 100 calls I have received, to ask the Secretary of State to remove the new 3 per cent tax on student loans, this unfair, discriminatory tax imposed on the poorer students who need to borrow for college and university education, one that needs to be paid up front and in cash.
Will the minister remove this brutal damaging tax today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Secretary of State of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to refer my hon. colleague to the answer I gave him last Monday on this issue.
The Canada Student Loan Program is a program introduced 27 years ago. It is under full review. The administrative costs have been rising very sharply. The 3 per cent has been imposed because of that rise in administrative costs. We are reviewing the whole program.
I have talked with the Canadian Federation of Students and within the very near future I will be proposing amendments to the program to cabinet, and I will be tabling those amendments in the House.

Hopefully, the tax will be removed, Madam Speaker.

When the minister was President of the Treasury Board, he introduced this new discriminatory 3 per cent tax on student loans and said that it would compensate for bad loans. Why impose this new tax when the vast majority of students do pay back their loans? Isn't this immoral, in any case insensitive and perhaps even illegal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Secretary of State of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will repeat in French what I said in English. This program was introduced 27 years ago and is now under full review. Obviously, it is going to be amended to reflect the current situation. These amend-
September 20, 1991

merits are about to be submitted to cabinet and will be tabled in the House.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister of youth.
On June 10 and September 17 last the minister in this House twice denied that there had been funding cuts to the SEED program.
Let us use the national capital region as an example. According to the minister's own figures, federal funding for the SEED program, which is a student summer employment program, has been cut in this region from a 1989 level of $1.4 million to $424,000 in each of the last two years, a 70 per cent reduction. Hundreds of students could not find jobs in this region.
Will the minister reinstate funding to at least the 1989 level?

I ask the minister again: In preparation for next year's budget, will the minister reinstate the moneys to enable the youth of our region to have some hope for better job opportunities in 1992?

Oral Questions MULTICULTURALISM

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
The rise in racial violence and multicultural intolerance in Canada was inflamed this past summer by the Conservative convention resolutions. Will the government implement these resolutions which stated that the multicultural department should be closed down and multicultural funding should be cut?
If not, will the Acting Prime Minister on behalf of the government affirm today what it intends to do to promote greater understanding of multiculturalism and to implement the Multicultural Act actively?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the member for the opportunity to reinforce the commitment of the government.
The new department was confirmed on April 21, and I serve as the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. We have been very active in promoting the vision that I know the member is very supportive of, to help Canadians understand how important our diversity is and how it contributes to strengthen and enrich this nation.
More and more our program areas have been working to combat racism and racial discrimination and work to promote equality, equality of opportunity. The basic right of all Canadians is the opportunity to participate. Of course our programs of integration are working very well, our citizenship courts, the pride we all have in our citizenship. Just watch our continuing efforts as we go across the country, building important partnerships with all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I think it is incumbent on the Prime Minister to reaffirm his policy on behalf of the government as a whole. It is a very serious concern to people.
The Manitoba native justice inquiry and racial incidents in Halifax and Montreal this past summer are evidence that problems are very serious and that the federal government must act more aggressively to enforce minority rights and eliminate racism.
I ask the minister: Will the government initiate a major public education campaign and also establish a representative citizens' panel to investigate causes of racism, to

September 20, 1991
Oral Questions
consult with minority communities and make recommendations for government action?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Minister of Multicuituralism and Citizenship):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is this government that began the whole March 21 initiative some three years ago, which is a national awareness program to help Canadians understand the devastating effects of racism and the need to erase it from our society.
In fact, last March 21 we were pleased to welcome one of our very important partners, the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, an idea that had its birth in British Columbia, in the hon. member's province, and it contributed some $10 million of support to a very active program to help Canadians understand the benefits of our diversity.

Madam Speaker, this week we saw charges against 15 individuals dropped after they had been approved by a justice of the peace. The crown attorney involved in the case described some of the charges as a gross miscarriage of justice.
I recognize the value of private prosecutions in our justice system, but will the Attorney General review section 507 of the Criminal Code in order to ensure that this type of abuse of process does not happen to any individual again?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not sure that the difficulty that we saw described so graphically by the Attorney General of Ontario arises necessarily from the statute but more with how it is implemented.
As a British Columbian, I can say that these matters are handled very differently in my own province from the way they are handled in Ontario. I believe they are also handled very differently in Quebec and in Alberta.
What I have indicated is that this is a subject that I would like to see discussed by all of us who have the responsibility for the enforcement of the criminal law-I have it in the territories; my provincial colleagues have it
in the provinces-to ensure that a device which I think is an important part of a democratic justice system is not used to create injustices. I think that could probably be done without legislative change but with great care in the role taken by our prosecutors.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice.
When Mrs. Joyce Milgaard met the Prime Minister recently and asked about her son's wrongful conviction, he said he would look into it right away which gave Mrs. Milgaard a good deal of hope.
In the House of Commons on Thesday, the minister said that the Prime Minister merely said that he would look into the state of his health, which I think is veiy cruel and misrepresents what actually took place.
This case must be reopened. I want to ask the minister: When is she going to stop playing God and reopen the David Milgaard case?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, I have looked very closely not only at the comments of the Prime Minister but at subsequent comments of Mrs. Milgaard which confirm the Prime Minister's commitments with respect to David Milgaard's health. I have already indicated in the House the steps that were taken.
The Prime Minister I think had a very humanitarian concern and communicated with me immediately. I communicated with the people in Correctional Services Canada, and my understanding is that no request has been made by David Milgaard to change his location.
I do not play God with these applications. I am bound by the law and by evidence. I will review every application that comes to me on that basis as fairly and equitably as possible.
The first application that came to me did not meet the threshold. If another one that comes does, it will be granted. If it does not, it will not.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate today. This legislation sets up a special fund or a special account within the government accounts to receive in part the huge revenue overruns from the goods and services tax. The government at one time led us to believe that this tax would be revenue neutral. Now we find out that through deceit or incompetence the goods and services tax is yielding far more revenues than the government was willing to admit to the Canadian people and these revenues are flowing into the general accounts of the country.
It creates a problem for the government when it is intent, based on its Tory ideology of cutting back programs in health care and social services and education, to cry poverty in order to justify the cutbacks in these social programs. I guess it is a bit embarrassing when these huge volumes of revenue are flowing in through the goods and services tax, which the government denied was going to happen. Now people are justifiably arguing that if there is a surplus of revenues, how can it justify cutting
September 20, 1991

back on those social programs, when the revenues of the country are increasing.
Many of the things this government does are reminiscent of the old days of Social Credit in British Columbia and some of the financial stunts pulled there by the government in order to justify the continuation of that right wing conservative cost-cutting ideology it used, not necessarily to try to control the finances and balance the books, but to serve its ideology, which is to cut programs designed to serve people and at the same time reduce the tax burden and the regulatory burden on the people who serve them. That is the corporations and the wealthy families of Canada.
The Social Credit in British Columbia set up what they called "rainy day funds." This was so that they could set revenues in these special funds and bring them out during a rainy day. Well, of course, under the Social Credit it was always rainy in British Columbia and the finances were always in a situation that could be called "rainy day." Unfortunately, it was never rainy enough for the Socreds to use these special funds in order to serve the purposes they were set up to serve.

Well, I will get into that later on.
In fact a most recent example of this kind of budgetary flim flam was the so-called budget stabilization fund which was set up by one of the Ministers of Finance who have gone through the revolving door of that office in British Columbia over the last little while. It was called the budget stabilization fund, or as these things are commonly abbreviated, the BS fund, which more appropriately names the fund.
The account is designed to serve two purposes, as members will know. The first purpose is to set up an accounting fiction so that the government can take its surplus revenues and put it in this account so that it will not be seen by the public as being available for expenditure on social programs.
What the government does is it takes the cash in that special account and by selling the account treasury notes, it gets the cash back into general revenue where it is spent. We have had a couple of examples recently such as the $273 million KAON project in British Columbia on the threshold of a provincial election where the

Conservatives are trying to help their friends the Socreds in British Columbia to get re-elected in spite of all the things they have done in the past five years.
It was suggested by some of our members last night who were asking for aid for the farmers in the prairie provinces to assist them to overcome some of the problems of world market conditions and the conflict of subsidies that were taking place that payments be made to the farmers immediately rather than waiting until the time that it was most politically expedient so that the government could support its crony out there, Grant Devine, to try to get him elected. Therefore, the purpose of the aid to the farmers is more to elect Grant Devine than to provide any kind of assistance to agriculture in Saskatchewan.
The Socreds used the funds for the same kind of purpose. They used to stash away money into special funds, or rainy day funds, or political slush funds. When it came close to election time they took the money out of those funds and used it to improve their chances of getting re-elected.
This time I do not think they are going to be that successful. I am convinced they are not going to be that successful, so we will see an end to this kind of nonsense at least in the province of British Columbia.
There is a second purpose for the use of these kinds of funds and accounts, this flim-flam accounting, which is to deceive the people of Canada as to the actual volumes of revenue which are flowing into the federal treasury. The government would like to, because it has embarked on a cost-cutting program, cut programs in education, in health care, in social services, cut services to women and unemployed workers and training programs and that kind of thing. It wants people to believe that there is actually a tight revenue expenditure situation in this country.
It diverts a substantial amount of the revenue generated by the goods and services tax into this special fund and it is able to tell the public: "Sorry, you can't have a national child care program because the money is already spoken for. Sorry, you can't have a literacy program that is designed to achieve the objective of cutting illiteracy in this country in half by the year 2000 so that maybe we can approach the literacy rate of Mexico. We can't do that because the money has already been designated into this fund to pay off Canada's debt".

September 20, 1991
Government Orders
The idea is to keep the revenue and expenditures as close as possible so that people will not be able to petition the government to set up programs like child care, which the government has been promising for the last few years.
This goods and services tax will probably bring in sufficient revenues over this year to pay for the full cost of that program. What the government has to do is divert those revenues into this debt payment fund so that it will not have to pay for the child care program it has been promising for years and years and years.
It is a method of deceiving the people of this country using the kind of economic flim-flam through special accounts and special funds that the province of British Columbia under Social Credit has been using for years and years and years.
Anybody who understands British Columbia politics, surely most people west of the Rocky Mountains in this country, are going to understand that this is flim-flam. They are not going to believe it and it is not going to work.
I have a second concern about this proposal to set up a special fund in which to put all the surplus GST revenues or the revenues from selling Crown corporations and other revenues which may come to the government from other sources. That is that it does not address the real causes of the debt. While we may be putting these funds into the debt payment account, the real causes of the debt are still operating to increase the debt of Canada.
As one of our members pointed out this morning, when the Conservatives came into office in 1984 the debt of the country was $180 billion. In a recent report by the Department of Finance that debt load has now risen to over $400 billion. Under the Tories, from 1984 to 1991, the debt has risen from $180 billion to $400 billion.
It has more than doubled now to the point where the debt of each and every Canadian man, woman and child is $15,000. That is the accomplishment of the Tory government over the last decade, to double the debt and saddle $15,000 on to every man, woman and child in this country. That is the Tory record.
Statistics Canada did a recent study that was suppressed by the Tory government because it did not want the results to come out. That study showed what the causes of the debt actually were.
Frances Russell released the study in the Winnipeg newspapers back in March of this year. She talked about the suppressed Statistics Canada study which indicated that 44 per cent of Canada's national debt is not due to program spending. It is not due to runaway expenditures on such programs as health, education and welfare.
According to StatsCan's study, 44 per cent of Canada's debt is due to tax concessions to large corporations and wealthy individuals. That is one of the roots of the debt problem in this country.
This legislation does not address that problem. While we are setting up this fund, while we are paying the GST into this fund, and while we are paying revenues from the privatization of corporations into this fund, the real root of the problem is not being dealt with at all. That debt is going to increase and increase until the government actually deals with the root of the problem.
The second major contributor to the debt, according to Statistics Canada, in fact responsible for 50 per cent of Canada's public debt, is the high interest rate policy. Both of these policies, tax concessions to corporations and tax giveaways to corporations, were pursued by both the Liberal and the Conservative governments over the last three decades.
The high interest rate policy is the same. It has been pursued by Liberal and Tory governments over at least the past two decades. According to Statistics Canada, it is that high interest policy which is responsible for something like 50 per cent of the total public debt in Canada, that huge mushrooming debt which has reached over $400 billion under the Tories, or $15,000 for every man, woman and child in this country.
There are two issues. First, tax concessions to corporations which account for 44 per cent of the debt, and second, the high interest rate policy that causes that debt to mushroom is responsible for 50 per cent of the debt.
What about the social programs that the Tories like to talk about and the Socreds in British Columbia like to
September 20, 1991

talk about? What about those social programs that are accused by those political parties of being the major cause of our debt in this country?
According to the Statistics Canada study, which the Tories attempted to suppress, program spending accounts for only 6 per cent of the total debt problem in this country.
If program spending is only 6 per cent of the problem, why do the Tories haul out 100 per cent of their big guns to deal with that problem and leave the problem of interest rates alone? Why do they leave the problem of generous tax concessions to corporations alone?
Why do we not deal with the real issues, the things that are the root of this debt problem, root them out, solve those problems and reduce the debt that way?
Of course, that counters Tory ideology. We run up against a bit of an ideological road-block. If there is one thing that justifies the existence of Tories, it is cutting programs. They love to cut programs.
It does not matter whether we have good times or bad times in this country. Tory times are always bad times. In good times or in bad times Tories love to cut programs, in particular social programs. How have they opted to deal with the national debt? They have attacked transfer payments to the provinces. Most of those transfer payments go to pay for health care, social services, education, post-secondary education, programs and services that are needed by people all across Canada. These are programs that are very difficult to cut without decreasing the standard and quality of life in this country. Yet those are the programs the Tories have targeted with 100 per cent of their big guns.
Why not attack the problem of corporate tax concessions? We see all across this country the difficulty people are experiencing in shouldering the burden of taxes that Tories have loaded on them over the past decade. Income taxes, excise taxes, sales taxes, all the taxes that people pay have increased dramatically. People in the small business sector are complaining about the huge burden of taxes that the Socreds and Tories have placed on them. I hope this is not reported in British Columbia. If so, I withdraw the name Socred.
People all across the country are complaining about the burden of taxes that this Tory government has

This is a marketing plan and a marketing game by the present government. It is saying to Canadians that it is going to take special money and use that money to pay against the deficit. First Canadians were told, back when the government started to talk about the GST, that it would be revenue neutral, that as a country we were going to do away with the federal tax that was there before and replace it with a goods and services tax. It is raising more than that in a recession, so it is quite obvious that if and when-and hopefully that is soon-the economy turns around, it is going to be a cash cow. Some of the government members said that right from the start, and I applaud them for their honesty. Now I think they had their knuckles rapped by the powers that be in their caucus, but they were honest enough to tell Canadians that.
Naturally, if this account, if that section of income from the Canadian government brings in an extra $3 billion or $4 billion or whatever the case may be, where else would it go? Why would it not be applied against the bills that the government has? One of those bills is the interest. If we pay off a bigger section of our bills, then naturally the annual deficit of the country will be less.
So let us not be fooled by what is actually happening. I am very sceptical about what the government is telling Canadians, that they do not trust themselves to allow this to go into the regular funds in the regular bank account of the government, so they are going to put this in a separate account in order to make sure that they themselves keep themselves honest, if that is possible. They are saying that the only thing that account can be used for is to pay off some of the debts.
I hope that is the case because Canadians have become very sceptical. I hope that the government shows Canadians that they are not going to use that for patronage handouts and to come up with election promises as time goes on. That is what Canadians are saying, Mr. Speaker, that if the GST raises $4 billion or $5 billion more than the government has been up front in telling Canadians it is going to raise, it will put $2 billion or $3 billion of that against the deficit and take the other $1 billion or $2 billion as an election comes close and come out with election goodies. That has been done before, and I can tell you that all of Canada is going to watch that.
All that being said, Mr. Speaker, I do recognize that we do have an extreme deficit problem in the country. The deficit is nearly 5 per cent of our gross domestic product and there are very few countries-probably only Italy-that has a higher annual deficit in proportion to the gross domestic product than does Canada. That is the serious problem we have to address.
Unfortunately, the present government has failed to live up to the promises it made prior to 1984 and in 1984. Quite frankly, had it done that, had it lived up to what it told Canadians it would do, had it lived up to the reason Canadians elected one of the highest-if not the highest-majorities in this House for any political party in Canadian history, we would not be in the problem we are in at the present time. Within 24 hours of getting elected, it got too concerned about getting elected another time and said: "Okay, here goes the patronage and here come the handouts".
Canada went through six years of the best times this country has ever gone through. Any sound business or company would take advantage of the opportunity when they are making money to pay off some of their bills. This government did not do that.
Instead of fulfilling the promise to Canadians to have the deficit down to $16 billion by 1991, where are we? We are predicting a $30.5 billion deficit again in this fiscal year. When we look at the figures that are coming out now, in the first four months, the Canadian deficit is over $12 billion. I can figure it out. That is over $3 billion per month and 3 times 12 means a $36 billion deficit, not $30.5 billion.
September 20, 1991

Some very highly regarded people in the banking industry are saying that in all honesty, we are probably heading toward a $35 billion deficit, not a $30.5. Therefore, we have to address that.
It is time for some accountability. It is time to look after that account which is going to be set up, albeit needlessly. But if the government wants to set it up, I will support the setting up of it, but I am still very sceptical of why the government feels it is necessary.
The government has to address the problems that we have in this country and spend the money wisely. In its agenda it declared a number of years ago what had to be addressed. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand here and share this time with my colleague. I am delighted to have an opportunity to speak to Bill C-21 which is before us this afternoon and which is an act relating to the accounting of certain payments for the servicing and reduction of the debt in Canada. At the same time I am pleased to speak to this, I am somewhat sceptical of the government's motives. But I was pleased when in the February budget we were told they would create a fund which would credit all revenues from the GST, all proceeds from privatization and all gifts to Canada would be placed in an account for the purposes of reducing and servicing the debt.
I think not just I but all Canadians rejoiced at that planned initiative of the government.
The constituents in my riding have always expressed to me their particular concern about servicing, reducing, and eliminating the debt so I am pleased that I am able to present their collective views today. I am pleased to offer in this House my support in principle to Bill C-21 at second reading so that it can go to committee and be closely scrutinized. I mentioned earlier that I am also sceptical about the ability of this act to actually reduce the debt.
My scepticism flows from the government's dismal record on bringing forth the kind of responsible fiscal policy that it has always tried to claim as its trademark. The government in 1989 introduced a very ambitious five-year fiscal plan to begin the work of getting rid of the deficit and eventually the debt. What happened? As we know, in 1988-89 we had an operating deficit of $28.7 billion, in 1989-90 a deficit of $30.5 billion, and we are expecting $30.5 billion in 1991-92. The operating deficit has risen nearly $2 billion.
Herein lies my scepticism. Under this new ambitious plan of deficit and debt reduction of which Bill C-21 is a part, how much of a tab will the government run up in the next few years?
We already know that this new account itself will be in a deficit of at least $20 billion per year for the next five years. The deficit has continued to go up and down. During the years this government has been in power, it should have been reduced in better times during the 1980s. It was not.
What happened during the 1980s? We know that this government took office in 1984. From the period 1984 to 1988, and it was just alluded to by the member from Broadview-Greenwood, this country saw unprecedented growth, higher than ever before in the history of this country. I know that my colleague mentioned $50 billion. My understanding was that it was considerably higher than that.
What did they do? Did they put any of this excess revenue beyond all their wildest dreams, excess revenue over anticipated revenue, against the debt? Not one penny of it went against the debt. What did they do? I would like to know because I have never seen an
September 20, 1991

accounting of it and I know that I and my colleagues, and certainly Canadians, would be most interested in seeing how that money was spent.
During 1984 to 1988 this government was certainly the last of the big time spenders.
This government has chosen over those years to stick it to Canadians when they are down. Between 1988 and the period we are in now, the economy is down. Inflation is high. Bankruptcies are soaring. People are out of jobs. They introduced the GST during a recession. They pursued a high dollar, a high-interest policy when people could barely, if at all, make ends meet.

The government should have been reducing the debt as I mentioned earlier during the 1980s, which were the good times, and using available resources to help people in the economy during the bad times.

Research and development: we should be expanding our industries here in Canada and yet we have withdrawn money and reduced our input financially.
Education: our young people are the biggest resource that this country has and yet moneys have been reduced drastically to the provinces in the area of education.

huge sum of money which sits in this account. I have yet to hear back from the minister.

Under section 80 of the Income Tax Act, his non-capital losses of preceding years wiped out any gain on the debt and he may in fact eventually have to pay tax on the full writedown that the bank gave him. In other words, the bank wrote off $30,000 worth of debt and said it could not be collected. They wrote it off but the income tax department, through section 80, may in fact still want to collect taxes on that because it considers that the writedown was income and wants its tax on that income even though he never saw it.
Several other producers are being assessed because of paper profits as well. For instance, one producer had to declare a capital gain after he transferred land to the bank, because the land had been purchased at a lower price many years ago than what the bank took it back at. Since his paper income is now over $50,000 because of the paper transaction of the new value of the land, he is subject to the clawback provisions and has to repay his family's tax allowance and child tax credit advances.
In other words, the man did not get any money for his land, but in the process of taking it back on him the bank showed the recovery value as more than what he had originally paid for it. The difference was considered to be a capital gain and that was applied against his income. The man has no money and needed those child tax credits and the family allowances. He in fact had spent the money and is now being asked to go find money to pay taxes on that because under section 80 of the Income Tax Act he is required to consider that as income. If this continues there is no way that he could even use the averaging provisions to get out of this, if we had a similar case in the future after block averaging is no longer available.
I have a similar case. A man was losing his farm. These things in my province take a couple of years of process because of the provincial laws that we have. We have had
them in effect ever since 1944. He had actually gone out to work one winter to raise some money to keep his family alive. He had worked for eight or ten months and then the job played out because he was working in the far north and when it starts to melt they lay everybody off. Madam Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to speak on Motion No. 81, presented by the member for Mackenzie. The motion is to consider the
September 20, 1991

advisability of reintroducing amendments to the Income Tax Act to allow some form of averaging.
One of the fundamental principles of our income tax system is that the tax burdens of Canadians should reflect their ability to pay. In other words, the proportion of the income paid in tax should increase with income. This is achieved mainly through a progressive tax rate structure with tax rates ranging from 17 to 29 per cent, as was alluded to by the hon. member.
Another fundamental principle is that ability to pay is measured on the basis of income earned or received in a year. Only in a very few cases, such as the lifetime capital gains exemption and the cumulative net investment loss rules, are income and personal circumstances of other years are taken into account.
When income of individuals fluctuates significantly from year to year, the total of the income taxes they pay over several years may be greater than if their income stream has been more constant over that period. This is because in those years when incomes were high, they are subject to higher marginal tax rates and thus pay a greater proportion of their income in tax. In such circumstances, averaging the income over a number of years would result in lower taxes each year, thus lowering the total tax burden over the period.
An understanding of the underlying objective of averaging measures is essential in considering the need for the reintroduction of explicit averaging measures such as those referred to by the hon. member for Mackenzie.
Equally crucial, however, is an understanding of the circumstances that may result in an individual's income fluctuating over a lifetime. Specifically, who is most subject to those fluctuations, in what circumstances and how does the tax system currently treat those individuals.
It is not my intention to review all of the circumstances in which Canadians may experience large year over year changes in their incomes. The hon. member has referred to farmers. Madam Speaker, you may be more familiar with the fluctuations in the incomes of artists or performers.
However, I believe that most would agree that retirement is the most frequent and significant cause of such a
Private Members' Business
change. At retirement the vast majority of Canadians experience a reduction in their incomes.
I would like to take this opportunity to remind members of the existing tax assisted measures for retirement saving and the improvement to the system adopted by this House last summer as part of a major series of pension reforms that have been introduced in recent years. All are aimed at improving the income security for Canadians in retirement.
Tax assistance for retirement pensions is based on a simple principle. Within limits, amounts set aside for retirement should not be taxed when saved, but rather when received as pension income. Thus, tax assistance for pensions allows averaging of income between higher income years when an individual is working, is employed and low income year of retirement. The benefits of this averaging are compounded by the fact that the investment income earned on retirement savings is not taxed until income is paid out after retirement. The result is a significant reduction in the over-all tax burden to retired individuals.
These tax advantages are extremely important in providing income security for Canadians in retirement. They also represent costs to the federal and provincial governments.
For the federal government, these advantages to individuals amount to $5 or $6 billion a year and for the provinces, an additional $3 billion a year.
I noticed last year this House adopted changes which improved tax assistance for retirement. These changes had two key objectives; to increase the fairness of the system and to make it more flexible.
To increase fairness, the new system established uniform limits on the tax assistance for all Canadians. The benefits are now the same whether a pension saving is measured in terms of contributions or promised benefits and whether it takes place in one plan or more than one. Over a career the new limits will allow individuals to save, free of tax, amounts sufficient to provide annual retirement income amounting to 60 to 70 per cent of what they earned before retiring
In fact, these measures allow Canadians to average their incomes between active and retirement years to benefit from the associated reduction in tax.

To increase the flexibility of the system, last year's reform also introduced a new carry forward provision. As we know, it is not always possible to put aside a set proportion of earnings for retirement each year. Circumstances such as a temporary reduction in income, purchase of big ticket items or unforeseen expenditures may prevent individuals from saving as much as they would like through tax assisted retirement saving vehicles. Prior to these reforms, the unused contribution room was lost if that room was not used in a given year. However, the enactment of these changes to the Income Ihx Act means that taxpayers are now able to carry forward unused deductions for up to seven years.
Many Canadians, especially those starting out in employment or facing fluctuations in earnings for any reason, will find the new carry over provisions of unused RRSP contribution room a great advantage. Similarly, the flexibility for those who lose or change jobs will help them maintain their pension savings.
The new higher contribution limit to the RRSP-$15,500 in 1995-will be of particular benefit to self-employed individuals. Farmers, for example, will be able to mitigate the tax consequences of year by year fluctuations in their incomes while at the same time saving for retirement.
In closing, I would like to stress that as a result of the changes adopted last year, the system of tax assistance for retirement saving is second to none in the world. It provides millions of Canadians with the opportunity to provide equally and adequately for themselves in their retirement. It also provides all Canadians, including those with large year over year fluctuations in incomes a vehicle through which they can average their incomes over their lifetime and benefit from the associated reduction in their tax burden.
I think it is clear, Madam Speaker, that the objective set out in Motion 81 is largely met by the current tax assistance system for retirement savings embodied in the Income Tax Act.

Madam Speaker, I would like to salute the member for Mackenzie as well. At least, I think the member for Calgary Southeast was saluting the member for Mackenzie.
The sophistry, Madam Speaker, that we just heard from the member, and I say this with respect, having
known the member for a long time, but I think I detected a speech that was being read, rather than being given spontaneously, but I was too polite on a Friday afternoon to get up and ask him to stop reading a speech that no doubt he prepared, rather than somebody in the Department of Finance.
I would like to pick up a thread that was made, I think, yesterday by a member. Right now the average farmer in Canada produces food for about 95 to 100 Canadians. At the same time, since most farmers are men, his spouse has to go off the farm to earn money to feed the family on the farm. That, Madam Speaker, is a catastrophe. I am sure it is the case in Quebec, but I know it is the case in parts of Alberta, throughout Saskatchewan and throughout Manitoba and throughout much of Ontario.
I think it is in that spirit that the member for Mackenzie has put the motion. We simply have to do something to help farm families who are not going to be here too many years if we do not do things like this proposal to help them.
You probably saw, Madam speaker, the Canadian Press report that came out earlier this week saying that family incomes from 1980 to 1988 have gone down in Canada, down after taxes from $40,200 to $40,000. I might point out too, Madam Speaker, that the share of after tax income going to the 10 per cent of families with the highest incomes rose to 22.4 per cent from 21 per cent in that period, while the share going to the lowest 10 per cent of Canadians also increased to 2.9 per cent from
2.5	per cent.
The 32, 33, or 34 tax increases we have had from those opposite have obviously had a significant effect on the plight of the Canadian family, including of course, farm families. The fact that people in parts of Canada are suffering enormously through the various policies of the government, including high interest rates, higher and higher taxes on middle and low income Canadians, is something I think should disturb everyone in this House.
Madam Speaker, I would refer you, if I could, to another matter that recently came up, which was a statement by Statistics Canada in June that 58 per cent of married Canadians have less disposable income after taxes than if they lived in a common law relationship. I
September 20, 1991

believe most members would agree that marriage should be encouraged by any prudent national government and not penalized as it is now in our country.
Tax reform, as we heard from the member for Broadview-Greenwood today should mean-and I think he means-moving some of the present burden away from those who cannot afford to pay more and more taxes, middle and low income Canadians, to those who can, successful firms and high income individuals.
As I said before, there have been 32 or 33 tax increases by this government since 1984. In closing I would simply say I hope that all members here-there are members here, Madam Speaker, in the House this afternoon-will see fit to vote for this motion when it comes for a vote, particularly because it will help the farmers in western Canada that the member for Mackenzie and I try to represent.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak this afternoon to Motion No. 81 in the name of the hon. member for Mackenzie, which concerns the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so that taxpayers will be able to average their income when it fluctuates over a certain number of years.
Before 1988, the Income Tax Act contained two provisions for averaging income over a number of years: forward averaging and block averaging. Both methods were based on complex calculations and allowed taxpayers whose income fluctuated substantially to average their income tax over a number of years.
More specifically, individuals whose income in a year exceeded 110 per cent of their average adjusted income of the preceding three years could chose to average the excess.
Averaged income was deductible in computing taxable income but gave rise to a special tax at the highest marginal rate of the year. In subsequent years, the averaged amount was brought back and taxed as regular income with a refundable credit provided at the top marginal rate. Furthermore, before 1988, individuals whose chief source of income was farming or fishing could average income from all sources over a five-year
Private Members' Business
period. This provision involved a calculation whereby the taxpayer recalculated tax liability as if one-fifth of his or her total income over the period had been earned in each of the five years. An election to block average was made in the last year of the five-year period and reduced taxes payable in that year or resulted in a refund of taxes paid in the earlier years of the period.
As hon. members are aware, in 1988, the government proceeded with a reform of personal and corporate income tax. The purpose of personal income tax reform was to make Canada's tax system more equitable, strengthen our competitive position and stimulate growth and job creation.
The reform provided for lower tax rates and a broader tax base. The lower rates demanded by hon. members opposite stimulate employment and investment, which helps improve our standard of living.
A broader tax base, achieved by eliminating special tax benefits, makes our tax system less complex and more equitable, in addition to limiting opportunities for fiscal planning by mainly wealthy Canadians, something the hon. member for Mackenzie has always criticized.
So, starting in 1988, the old system with its 10 tax rates from 6 to 34 per cent was replaced by a three-rate structure: 17, 26 and 29 per cent. Another key element of this reform was the conversion of personal exemptions into often increased tax credits. Contrary to the exemptions, which tended to favour high-income earners-something the opposition always denounced-the credits are fairer in that they provide equal tax relief across the board. The third major change was the elimination or reduction of many tax benefits. For instance-and this affects businesses and business owners-tax deductions for business expenses such as meals and entertainment were considerably limited.
Because of the fewer tax rates and income brackets, the opportunity of the forward averaging provisions was called into question and eventually abolished as part of the tax reform. Income averaging has not been allowed since the 1988 tax year, while the averaging provisions relating to farm producers and fishermen do not apply to five-year periods starting after 1987. The averaged amounts deducted previously can be added to the year's income until 1997 and the taxpayer will remain eligible to

September 20, 1991
Private Members' Business
a federal tax credit at the current marginal tax rate at that time.
Let us now examine, Madam Speaker, why it is that the new tax rates and the fewer income brackets resulting from the tax reform make the averaging provisions less relevant. Before the reform, there was a 28 percentage point difference between the lowest tax rate (6 per cent) and the highest (34 per cent). It was huge. Thus, there were huge variations in the tax paid by taxpayers whose income fluctuated from one year to the next. With the reform, the difference between the minimum (17 per cent) and maximum (29 per cent) tax rates was reduced to 12 percentage points. So, fluctuations in revenue are less likely to noticeably affect the tax burden.
Combined to the conversion of exemptions into tax credits, the fewer rates enhanced the fairness and progressive character of the tax system.
Doing away with the averaging provisions also helped simplify the system as well as compensate for the reduction in the number of tax rates.
While there are no averaging provisions in the current system, strictly speaking, income and tax can easily be deferred under other provisions.
More particularly, tax assistance for retirement savings has enabled taxpayers to spread their income over the years in which they earned it and those following their retirement. Tax assistance is based on the principle that retirement savings are taxed when they are withdrawn and not when they are accumulated. This means that someone who has a very large income today can obtain the maximum, as my colleague just explained, and enjoy it later, at the same time paying much less tax on it.
Therefore, contributions to registered retirement savings plans (RRSPs), registered retirement plans and deferred profit sharing plans are not taxable when they are paid. Similary, investment income in these plans is not taxed as it is earned. Retirement savings are taxable only when benefits are paid by the plan. For the great majority of taxpayers whose retirement income, and thus marginal tax rate, is lower, tax-assisted retirement savings are a good way to spread income and defer tax.
As you know, Madam Speaker, the limits on tax assistance for retirement savings were recently changed. The new regime that takes effect this year corrects all
the shortcomings of the old system and gives Canadians fairer access to tax-assisted retirement savings. Before the reform, taxpayers whose employment situation was different did not enjoy the same level of tax assistance. More particularly, those whose employer did not provide a pension plan could not benefit from tax assistance in setting up an adequate retirement fund. Those with relatively modest pension plans could contribute more to an RRSP than taxpayers with a very good pension plan.
I believe this was a satisfactory response to the demands of our friends opposite who during the past few years have constantly asked for a fairer and more equitable system that would take more from the rich and give more to the poor. The tax reform does just that.
Because of the current limits, the number of tax planning measures available has tended to increase. Before, some taxpayers did not have access to appropriate tax assistance while others benefited to an extent that in some cases was downright outrageous.
The key element of the new system is this: A maximum of 18 per cent of income is eligible for tax-assisted retirement saving, regardless of the type of plan.
Thanks to deferral of the unused portion of RRSP contributions, the new system will be more flexible and allow taxpayers to adapt retirement savings contributions to their current and future financial needs.
This will be of particular interest to taxpayers whose income fluctuates. The new limits will eliminate the barriers that prevent many individuals from taking advantage of tax-assisted retirement saving. They promote autonomy and encourage people to save now for tomorrow's retirement.
Madam Speaker, I believe that the durable benefits of tax reform and the attractive prospect of income deferral offered by the new tax-assisted retirement saving system will respond more effectively to the needs of Canadians than would a number of complex averaging measures.
As you know Madam Speaker, in the past governments have been criticized for the unfair aspects of the system. The richer you were, the less taxes you paid, and the poorer you were, the more you paid. This tax reform helps to avoid the incredible differences that existed in the past. In fact, I am surprised the NDP member for
September 20, 1991

Mackenzie should wish to reinstate a system that was abolished at their urgent request.
Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I want to salute the member for putting this motion forward on income averaging. I think, as you said earlier today Madam Speaker, this has been a good afternoon because we have been focusing on an issue which I think is priority one in this country. I salute the member who is bringing to the forefront an issue which is not only of concern to farmers.
In my riding, Broadview-Greenwood, which is downtown Toronto, there are many people in the motion picture industry, artists, and entertainers. This is an industry where it is either feast or famine, it can be a terrific year. It is the home of Degrassi Junior High, and we have many large film studios in the riding. This problem about income averaging is talked about all the time. We have many entertainers in our riding. Our riding is the home of Kim Mitchell, a Juno Award winner, who decided last year decided to do a lot of touring. He had exceptional success and a couple of good hits. Of course he had a balloon year in terms of his income, as Blue Rodeo, who are from my riding, did the year before.
This is an area where, not only farmers but also artists, really have to put a tight focus on income averaging. This goes back to the point that many of us in the House were making earlier, and that is fairness. Being an artist can be a tough, lonely grind. Quite often people go many years, thousands of hours, when they do not make anything. They work from hand to mouth, pay cheque to pay cheque. It is a very tough game. Then all of a sudden they have a successful year. It seems that the averaging concept is not really addressed.
I salute the hon. member for this. I hope that we can get this idea to a point where we can not only deal with it in a fair way but also in a simple and efficient way.
It has been a strange afternoon in terms of tax reform because things react so quickly in the country now with fax machines. As we were talking this afternoon about
Private Members' Business
tax reform and fairness in the tax system, I received a fax from the Toronto Construction Association. It is pleading with all of us in this House, not only about averaging but also concerning the payroll deductions the minister has currently put forward in his latest budget and the fact that he is not allowing the provincial payroll tax to be deducted under the federal system.
The Toronto Construction Association, which is on its knees right now because of a lack of activity, is begging us in this House to plead with the minister and his officials in finance to review this situation. I will send over the letter from Mr. Roly Nicholls, the chairman of the board and vice-chairman of the Toronto Construction Association, and ask the minister to hear their plea concerning fairness for their sector.
It has been a constructive afternoon. I hope we can continue to put this hon. member's motion forward to the next stage.

Madam Speaker, I want to compliment my colleague from Mackenzie for trying to get reinstated, starting next year, something that has long been of benefit to many thousands of farmers, fishermen and entertainers since the early 1950s.
When I was a station agent in a little prairie town in the 1950s and early 1960s, I did income tax returns for many farmers. In one year they would have a gross income of $10,000 or $12,000 and that would happen one, two or three years in a row, mainly because of low quotas and no boxcars and that sort of thing, or the quality of the crop. Then in 1952 we had a bumper high grade crop and incomes jumped up to $30,000, $40,000 to $50,000. The fact that they could average saved them thousands of dollars in income tax. In some of those years when they got little or no crop, they had to pay little or no income tax.
As a result of the very nature of agriculture, the fishery and the entertainment industry, incomes fluctuate wildly, from year to year to year. There is nothing new about that.
I listened to the minister of grains and oilseeds yesterday when he was responding to the NDP opposition day motion, again moved by my colleague the hon.

September 20, 1991
Private Members' Business
member for Mackenzie, in which he wept as many or more tears as anybody else in the House about the plight of agriculture and what a tough time farmers were having. He railed against the European Community and the American subsidies. He said: "We have got to do everything we can do".
Most of what he said none of us could disagree with. We have to do everything we can to ease the burden, no matter how small or large, on the agricultural industry.
While he was making his speech the government's law does away with five-year averaging for farmers, fishermen and entertainers. It does away with it. That is some way to help agriculture. Is that what he means by doing all we can do to help agriculture?
I had understood the government was going to call for third reading today on the bill concerning the At and East freight rates. However, there is some fuss being made about that in New Brunswick. There is an election on in New Brunswick so it has been put off. It will not be called until next week at the soonest.
The At and East freight rates have meant an up to $40 million a year benefit for grain producers. It meant a benefit to Saint John and Halifax in milling wheat and flour. It was a benefit to Halifax in feed grains.
Is this the way the government is going to do all it can to help agriculture? By doing away with the At and East freight rates? It is a benefit to both grain producers and the ports of Saint John and Halifax.
The terminal at Saint John has already closed down. It has been closed for a year. Is that what the minister means by "doing all we can to help agriculture". I think it happened a year and a half or two years ago. We had what was called a two-price system in which we charged ourselves-Canadians charged Canadians-anywhere from $6 to $10 a bushel for grain consumed in Canada for human consumption.
That was the one area where the farmer got his cost production and some profit. That meant up to $200 million a year for grain producers. What did the Tories do? The minister of grains and oilseeds just sat and took it. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture, who have been there and are prairie farmers, did not say a word.
There goes up to $200 million a year of benefit for western grain producers. Is that what the minister means by "doing all we can to help"? There is the bridge rate, the movement of grain by rail cars in the winter months from Thunder Bay east. That is no longer available.
Is that what the government means? Is that what the minister of grains and oilseeds means about doing all we can to help? I can recite a list of items as long as your arm that the government of this day has done over the last several years to hurt agriculture, and in particular the grain industry.
For example, freight rates. I remember the hon. member for Vegreville, the member for Kindersley- Lloydminster, and the then member for Swift Current-Maple Creek screaming just as loud as I did when the Liberals did away with the Crow rates. We fought that battle for three years against the Liberals.
The Tories take over and what do they do? They keep it. What has happened since the Tories came in? The freight charges for grain producers have gone up and up every year. Want to do something to help agriculture? Why not put a freeze on those freight rates? Why not say that there will be no increases until farmers are getting a price for their commodities that gives them the cost of production plus something to live on?
How about freezing those grain rates? How about keeping the At and East rates? How about restoring the two-price grain system? How about paying some of the storage costs in the terminal elevators in Vancouver, Thunder Bay, Prince Rupert and Churchill as the government used to do under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act? How about it? This is not any big, multibillion dollar subsidy, because we cannot compete with the treasuries of the European community and the United States. We know that.
There are a host of smaller items that when together mean something to our agricultural community. I am particularly surprised and flabbergasted that rural members in the Conservative Party would accept this government measure and not demand a reinstatement of the five-year averaging provisions. I do not understand them. As one of my aboriginal friends said: "They speak with a forked tongue. They have a hot mouth and a cold heart". That speech yesterday by the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds was a classic example of the hot mouth and cold heart of the government. There, is
September 20, 1991

absolutely no reason why it cannot allow averaging. It is not as though it is going to mean an horrendous loss in tax revenue for the federal treasury; the amount it will cost will be infinitesimal compared to the current deficit alone.
My hon. colleague for Papineau and I believe the previous government speaker got into retirement plans and the benefits there are to this. I suggest to those gentlemen that they go into their ridings and see if they can find a farmer who has any money to put into a retirement plan. I don't have any in my riding. They took a 30 per cent cut in their grain prices this year. You won't let them average and you are telling them they have all these benefits of putting money into retirement savings, up to 18 per cent of their income. Hell's bells, 18 per cent of their income is all of the net income they have to pay for their operations.
Madam Speaker, we can do no less than what the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds said we should do; that is, all we can. Well, this is one of the smaller items that will contribute to doing all we can for grain producers and fishermen, by restoring the averaging provisions.

Madam Speaker, I am delighted to have just a few moments to discuss this topic today, introduced by the hon. member for Mackenzie. Indeed, this member seems to have dominated the House, because all day yesterday we debated a motion on farm income that he had introduced.
Madam Speaker, today we have a person with cultural background in the Chair in yourself, and the speaker from Broadview-Greenwood was mentioning the cultural aspects. Indeed in my great riding I have the Stratford Shakespearian Festival. Culture and agriculture seem to go together today, as they always do in my riding.
In this motion that the member for Mackenzie has brought forward he is asking the government to consider the advisability of introducing amendments to the Income Tax Act so that taxpayers whose incomes fluctuate from one year to the next would be able to average their income over five years.
Well, it is a good motion and I can see the rationale for it. But it is similar to the five-year block averaging for
Private Members' Business
farmers and fishermen that was introduced in the Income Tax Act in 1946 and eliminated in 1988 as part of tax reform. Those provisions allowed individuals whose chief source of income was farming or fishing to average income over five year blocks. When income fluctuated significantly from year to year, block averaging reduced the total tax payable over the five-year period. This was particularly applicable to farmers whose income does vary a great deal because of drought, disease, or price fluctuations.
I must say that after the debate yesterday, and in fact after the many discussions we have had across Canada, that the member for Mackenzie, when thinking about averaging income for farmers must be thinking of better times. Because just lately it seems incomes have dropped rather than going up or ever going very high. So perhaps the member's concern is for farmers in the future.
Because I am only going to have a minute and I cannot really talk about the motion too much, I do want to set the record straight on some of the things the member from Regina said. He stood in this House just minutes ago and said how this government had taken away $40 million in benefits from the farmers through the At and East Program, a bill that is still to come before the House.
Well, Madam Speaker, there was a benefit for farmers in the At and East. It was about $8 million as I recall. The other $32 million was filtered off to transportation agencies and other people and not for the farmers- hardly an efficient way to spend government money to help farmers.
He talked as well about the two-price system and how we took $200 million out of the hands of the farmers. We studied that issue, I think, about five years ago. This two-price system, by the way, was first brought in to hurt the farmers because they were getting too much for their wheat and they wanted to have local wheat sold at lower prices. So, over the years it was off and on hurting or helping the farmers. At the end, of course, it was helping farmers but was, in turn, hurting the processing industry who had to compete with pasta made from our wheat shipped back into Canada. So it was helping the farmers, but hurting another sector of the Canadian industiy that really should not be allowed to be hurt.

Perhaps I could go back to discussing the motion for that minute I have left. I must say that block averaging was used only by 4 per cent of the farmers and fishermen. Hardly crippling, Madam Speaker, which was the way the member for Mackenzie introduced it. I assume it was used by the bigger and better farmers, farmers who would use all of the things associated with registered plans.
I am sure I have now expended my time so thank you for that little bit of time.
